results.corrected_extracted: Unweighted counts: 4,631 of 19,549 men and 3,121 of 19,263 women with an age at first drink in Table 1 have a time from first drink to dependence, 23.7% and 16.2% (editors' arithmetic; ratio 1.46); the first-drink counts total 38,812, more than the 38,309 lifetime drinkers analysed in Table 2, and the dependence counts total 7,752, fewer than the 8,564 people with dependence analysed in Table 2 (study card reporting issue), so the shares are approximate. For time from first drink to dependence, Table 1 marks no gender difference as significant in the cohorts born 1974–1983 (men 2.8, women 3.1 years), 1944–1953 (7.9, 8.6) and 1934–1943 (10.4, 11.8).
results.note: Arithmetic, cohort means and missing significance marks confirmed. The denominators are Table 1's initiation-column Ns, totalling 38,812, not Table 2's 38,309 lifetime drinkers; cohort-1 men's initiation N (2,634) even exceeds their total (2,553).

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized (Kaskutas et al., 2005): women were randomized to a women-only day programme with gender-specific content or to one of three mixed-gender day programmes (two community-based, one hospital-based); the only significant outcome differences were between the women-only and the hospital-based programme, which had higher total abstinence during follow-up and cost twice as much per week, so the women-only programme did not differ significantly from the two community-based programmes; the sample was small; the review, citing the trial, says the findings suggest that women may be equally well served by high-quality mixed-gender and women-only day programmes.
results.note: Details match the 6th paragraph. The closing suggestion carries a citation to Kaskutas et al. (2005), so it is attributed to the trial, not stated as the review's own conclusion; 'did not differ' means no significant difference.

Section 4.1, 5th paragraph matches (79.3% vs 54%; 'after controlling for greater length of stay'; women eliminated heavy-drinking days, men averaged four); whether the heavy-drinking difference was adjusted is not stated.

results.corrected_extracted: As summarized: nicotine dependence is the exception to the pattern of no gender difference, with worse outcomes in women; nicotine replacement worked better in men in a large randomized study; varenicline worked better in women in one meta-analysis and, in another of 32 trials (14,389 people, 51% women), as well in both sexes against placebo but with greater benefit for women relative to nicotine patch and bupropion; there is some evidence that with naltrexone for smoking, men reduced smoking more and women gained less weight. For other medicines, gender differences were not consistently shown: women responded worse to disulfiram for cocaine dependence; a poorer response in women has not been reported in trials of disulfiram for alcohol dependence, perhaps because women were badly under-represented (for example 1.2%); naltrexone for alcohol dependence gave mixed findings (men better under some dosing; no difference in COMBINE); no significant difference with buprenorphine or methadone; women did worse than men with buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine dependence, where buspirone did not beat placebo in either sex.
results.note: Numbers and findings match paragraphs 3–4. But the source says poorer response 'has not been reported' in alcohol disulfiram trials (not that trials report no difference), opioid agonist studies showed no significant differences, and naltrexone smoking findings are 'some evidence'.

Paragraphs 2 and 4 match. McHugh does not call Orwin et al. (2001) a meta-analysis here (Greenfield 2007 does), and paragraph 2 also reports Bride (2001), where switching to single-gender programming showed no better outcomes.

results.corrected_extracted: Table 1 values among people who use cocaine, taking the shorter window and powder over crack as the review did, run 23.5% to 87% (simultaneous alcohol), 9.3% to 76.5% (simultaneous cannabis), 34.9% to 96.5% (concurrent alcohol; Table 1's lifetime figures, left out by that rule, reach 98.3%) and 43.2% to 93.7% (concurrent cannabis). Editors' calculation (AI reader 288, agreeing with second reader 278's): DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling on the logit scale of these values, with the review's rules (shorter window, powder over crack), gives 37.9% (95% CI 19.7–60.3%) from 7 sources for simultaneous cannabis and 77.0% (62.1–87.2%) from 11 for concurrent alcohol, matching the printed 38% and 77%, but 70.1% (46.1–86.5%) from 8 for simultaneous alcohol and 66.5% (49.5–80.1%) from 8 for concurrent cannabis, against the printed 74% and 64%.
results.note: My DerSimonian–Laird logit recomputation reproduces all four editors' estimates, intervals and source counts exactly. But the concurrent-alcohol range holds only under the shorter-window rule: Table 1's lifetime figure among cocaine users reaches 98.3% (Rx study).
